name: Anabolic diet / high calorie eating

card.summary: A cyclic low-carbohydrate bodybuilding diet from the 1990s, often grouped with heavy-eating approaches to gaining size; no appearance studies found.
card.aka: Anabolic Diet, Pork Chop Diet, cyclic ketogenic diet
card.note: Sources for this entry are thin; no community discussion or trials were found.

quick.overview:
The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic diet described in a 1995 book by Mauro Di Pasquale, a Canadian powerlifter and writer. It was nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet.

It is grouped here with high-calorie eating for size. Little material specific to appearance was found, so this entry is short.
quick.mechanism: The diet is described as a cyclic ketogenic approach that alternates low-carbohydrate eating with higher-carbohydrate periods. Details of the claimed mechanism are not covered in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: No clinical studies were found, and the sources reviewed do not document risks specific to the diet.

lead: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic diet (CKD) described in Mauro Di Pasquale's 1995 book of the same name, nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet.[1] It is used by lifters who want to add muscle while staying lean, so the physique looks fuller without excess fat. Heavy or high-calorie eating more broadly means eating a calorie surplus to gain weight and muscle, known in bodybuilding as bulking.[2]

Di Pasquale, born in 1945, is an Italian-born Canadian powerlifter, author and low-carbohydrate advocate who won the IPF World Powerlifting Championships in 1976 and the World Games in 1981.[1] He later wrote The Metabolic Diet (2000) and worked as a drug-testing official in professional wrestling.[1]

Wikipedia describes a calorie surplus as the basis of bulking, with larger or longer surpluses adding more body fat, and clean bulks usually using moderate carbohydrate, moderate protein and low fat.[2] No study was found testing the Anabolic Diet for appearance outcomes.

chain: Fuel for heavy training and recovery
angle.text: Lifters use surplus eating, including cyclic low-carbohydrate approaches like the Anabolic Diet, to gain muscle and size. Larger surpluses tend to add more fat as well, so bulking is typically followed by a cutting phase.

paras: Di Pasquale advocates low-carbohydrate diets and wrote for the bodybuilding press; his books include Drug Use and Detection in Amateur Sports (1984), The Anabolic Diet (1995), Amino Acids and Proteins for the Athlete (1997) and The Metabolic Diet (2000).[1] He worked on writing, research and product development for supplement company EAS from 1997 to 1999.[1]

Wikipedia's bodybuilding article describes bulking as eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle, with the surplus size set by goals.[2] Clean bulking aims to add muscle with little fat and often alternates higher and lower calorie days, while dirty bulking involves a large surplus with little tracking and typically adds significant fat, needing a harder cut afterward.[2] Protein recommendations of 25 to 30 percent of calories are suggested but debated, and some bodybuilders eat five to seven meals a day to manage large food volumes.[2]

A content analysis of the 2009 issues of Men's Health found frequent advice to raise calorie intake (183 references) and protein intake (262 references) to augment muscle mass, described by the authors as an anabolic diet and framed within a mesomorphic body ideal.[3] On T Nation, members describe high-protein, high-fat eating and jokingly call steak and eggs the most anabolic diet.[5][6]

No studies found on the Anabolic Diet for appearance or muscle outcomes. A 1992 randomized trial gave 40 hyperlipidemic patients a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet it labelled anabolic, with or without pyruvate, and measured blood lipids and heart-rate parameters rather than muscle.[4]

timeline.event: Di Pasquale wins the IPF World Powerlifting Championships.[1]
Di Pasquale publishes The Anabolic Diet.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, the anabolic label is used loosely for high-protein, higher-fat or surplus eating.[5][6]

claims.claim: Steak-and-eggs style eating is the 'most anabolic diet'
claims.believers: A member posting in a confessions thread jokes that eggs and steaks may be the most anabolic diet ever.[5]
claims.experts: No trial reviewed tests this claim; the Men's Health content analysis notes dietary advice often relies on expert citations with little contextualisation.[3]

claims.claim: High-protein, high-fat eating works for body composition within days
claims.believers: One T Nation poster reported that a high-protein, high-fat diet was working after a few days.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that calorie balance sets whether a diet adds fat or muscle.[2]
